name: HAA299

lead: HAA299 is an experimental organic filter designed to absorb long-wave UVA (UVA-1) and the violet edge of visible light. Those wavelengths reach deep into skin and are linked to aging and pigmentation, so the payoff is less deep UV damage and less light-induced darkening.

It absorbs light at the boundary between ultraviolet and visible wavelengths, which can trigger pigmentation through oxidative stress. A small volunteer study reported protection against pigmentation induced at 385 and 405 nm, and the EU's SCCS issued an opinion on a nano form in 2021.

paras: It is intended for sunscreen products, particularly those targeting long-wave UVA and visible-edge light. It is not established as a marketed consumer ingredient in the sources reviewed, and benefits for aging would build over long-term use.
Human evidence is limited to a single small pigmentation study, and there are no long-term appearance trials. Safety was assessed by the SCCS for the nano form only; details are in the full opinion.

angle.text: HAA299 is an experimental sunscreen filter designed to cover long-wave UVA-1 and the violet edge of visible light, wavelengths linked to skin aging and pigmentation. It has a small early study and an EU safety-committee opinion.

lead: HAA299, with the INCI name bis-(diethylaminohydroxybenzoyl benzoyl) piperazine, is an experimental organic UV filter designed to absorb long-wave UVA (UVA-1) and the violet edge of visible light.[1][2] The EU's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) issued a scientific opinion on a nano form of HAA299 in 2021, describing it as a UV filter intended for sunscreen products to protect skin against UVA-1 rays.[2]
A 2022 study reported that a visible-light-absorbing filter of this type offered protection against pigmentation induced by wavelengths at the boundary of ultraviolet and visible light.[1]

paras: HAA299 is intended as a sunscreen active against UVA-1 radiation.[2] Its relevance to appearance is that solar ultraviolet radiation causes skin pigmentation, and visible light has also been shown to induce rapid pigmentation, a process thought to involve oxidative stress and linked to photoageing and skin cancer.[1]

The SCCS adopted a preliminary opinion on HAA299 (nano) in July 2021 and a final opinion in October 2021, published in a 2023 journal record.[2] The abstract available for this review describes the substance and its intended use; its safety conclusions are not summarised here.

A study of healthy volunteers with Fitzpatrick skin types II-IV irradiated the lower back with narrow-band 385 nm and 405 nm light at increasing doses and reported that the new filter gave superior protection against pigmentation at the ultraviolet-visible boundary.[1] No trials of consumer sunscreens containing HAA299 for long-term skin outcomes were found in the available literature.
